items.title: Today's lesson
items.content:
A stopping-distance puzzle opens the lesson: if a car goes **twice as fast**, how much more road does it need to stop?

One car on a highway then carries everything: its velocity–time graph gives all **three equations of motion**, each checked against the graph.

We end with braking numericals that answer the opening puzzle.

items.title: You already know
items.content:
• $a = \dfrac{v-u}{t}$, and km/h into m/s

• slope of a velocity–time graph = acceleration

• area under it = displacement

• area of a rectangle, a triangle and a trapezium

items.title: By the end, you can
items.content:
**1.** Derive $v=u+at$, $s=ut+\tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ and $v^2=u^2+2as$ from the graph.

**2.** Choose the right equation from what is given and asked.

**3.** Solve board-style numericals, including braking.

script.x: ONLY for you, not meant for students.

items.text:
**What this shows**

• A truck on a highway with **KEEP SAFE DISTANCE** on the back.

• The car behind is braking hard.

**Answer to Question 1**

A moving car cannot stop instantly — it needs some road to stop.

**Answer to Question 2**

Take a quick poll. Most will say 20 m. **Do not reveal the answer yet.**

**Answer to Question 3**

Yes — if we had an equation linking speed, braking and distance.

script.x: Show the highway. Pointer 1 sets it up.
Questions 1, 2 and 3 in order. Answers are on pointers 2, 3 and 4.
On Question 2, poll the room and move on — the answer comes back in Practice.
Show the conclusion box.

items.text:
**What this shows**

• A car on a highway, already moving at $10\ \text{m/s}$ at $t=0$ (point A).

• It speeds up uniformly and reaches $20\ \text{m/s}$ at $t=5$ s (point B).

• $BC = v-u$ and $AC = t$.

**Answer to Question 4**

$10\ \text{m/s}$. **No** — it is already moving. This is its initial velocity $u$.

**Answer to Question 5**

$\dfrac{BC}{AC} = \dfrac{20-10}{5} = 2\ \text{m/s}^2$ — the **acceleration**.

**Answer to Question 6**

By $a\times t$: here $2\ \text{m/s}$ every second, so $2\times 5 = 10\ \text{m/s}$ in 5 s.

script.x: Show the graph. Pointer 1 sets up what A, B and C are.
Questions 4, 5 and 6. Answers are on pointers 2, 3 and 4.
Show the derivation and work it line by line on the board.
Show the conclusion box.

items.prompt: A bus starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 0.5 m/s². Its velocity after 20 s is
A train moving at 20 m/s brakes with an acceleration of −0.5 m/s². Its velocity after 30 s is
True or false: v = u + at can be used for a car whose driver presses the accelerator harder and then softer.
options: True — it works for any motion
True — as long as the car speeds up
False — the acceleration is not uniform

items.text:
**On Question 2**

$v = 20 + (-0.5)(30) = 20-15 = 5\ \text{m/s}$, still in the direction of motion.

items.text:
**What this shows**

• The same graph, with the area under AB split in two.

• **Rectangle OACD** is $u\times t$.

• **Triangle ABC** is $\tfrac{1}{2}\,t\,(v-u)$.

**Answer to Question 7**

The **displacement**.

**Answer to Question 8**

$OA \times OD = 10 \times 5 = 50\ \text{m}$ — how far the car would go if it did **not** speed up.

items.text:
**What this shows**

• The same graph, with the area under AB split in two.

• **Rectangle OACD** is $u\times t$.

• **Triangle ABC** is $\tfrac{1}{2}\,t\,(v-u)$.

**Answer to Question 9**

$\tfrac{1}{2} \times AC \times BC = \tfrac{1}{2}\times 5\times 10 = 25\ \text{m}$ — the extra distance because it speeds up.

**Answer to Question 10**

$50 + 25 = 75\ \text{m}$.

items.prompt: A cyclist moving at 4 m/s accelerates uniformly at 1 m/s² for 6 s. How far does she go in this time?

Assertion (A): A car starting from rest with uniform acceleration covers four times as much distance in 10 s as in 5 s.  Reason (R): For u = 0, s = ½at², so the displacement grows with the square of the time.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

items.text:
**On Question 1**

$s = 4\times 6 + \tfrac{1}{2}\times 1\times 6^2 = 24+18 = 42\ \text{m}$.

items.text:
**What this shows**

• The **same** area, now read as one trapezium OABD.

• The parallel sides are $OA = u$ and $BD = v$.

• They are $t$ apart.

**Answer to Question 11**

**Neither** works directly — both of them need $t$.

**Answer to Question 12**

$\tfrac{1}{2}(u+v)\,t$.

items.prompt: A car moving at 20 m/s brakes with an acceleration of −5 m/s². How far does it go before stopping?
Why can't you find a stopping distance with v = u + at alone?
options: It does not contain s — it can only give the stopping time
It only works when a is positive
It needs the mass of the car

items.text:
**On Question 1**

It stops, so $v=0$:  $0 = 20^2 + 2(-5)s$, so $s = \dfrac{400}{10} = 40\ \text{m}$.

items.text:
**What this shows**

• The five quantities $u$, $v$, $a$, $s$, $t$.

• Each equation links four of them and **leaves one out**.

• The crossed-out circle is the one it leaves out.

script.x: Show the chart. Pointer 1 explains how to read it.
Show the key idea box.

items.text:
**Answer to Question 15**

$u=0$, $a=3$, $t=4$; find $s$; $v$ is left out, so $s = ut+\tfrac{1}{2}at^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\times 3\times 16 = 24\ \text{m}$.

**Answer to Question 16**

$u=0$, $v=14$, $a=9.8$; find $s$; $t$ is left out, so $v^2 = u^2+2as$ gives $s = \dfrac{196}{19.6} = 10\ \text{m}$.

**Answer to Question 17**

$u=25$, $v=0$, $a=-0.5$; find $t$; $s$ is left out, so $v = u+at$ gives $t = \dfrac{25}{0.5} = 50\ \text{s}$.

script.x: For each one: what is given, what is to be found, which quantity is left out?
Questions 15, 16 and 17. Answers are on pointers 1, 2 and 3.
Show the conclusion box.

items.prompt: A cyclist speeds up from 2 m/s to 8 m/s at 1.5 m/s². How long does it take?
A car at 30 m/s brakes at 6 m/s². How far does it go before stopping?
A ball rolls from rest at 2.5 m/s² for 4 s. How far does it roll?

items.text:
**On Question 1**

No $s$, so use $v=u+at$:  $t = \dfrac{8-2}{1.5} = 4\ \text{s}$.

**On Question 2**

No $t$, so use $v^2=u^2+2as$:  $s = \dfrac{900}{12} = 75\ \text{m}$.

**On Question 3**

No $v$, so use $s=ut+\tfrac{1}{2}at^2$:  $s = \tfrac{1}{2}\times 2.5\times 16 = 20\ \text{m}$.
